questions.prompt: Sami has already written "good" four times in the same paragraph and wants a different word for each one. Which book does he open?
questions.explanation: A thesaurus arranges words in groups according to sense and hands you the exhaustive list of equivalents: look up good and you get fine, excellent, admirable, decent, sound. A dictionary would only confirm a meaning Sami already knows, an encyclopedia describes subjects rather than words, and a grammar book deals with structures, not with word choice.

questions.prompt: English speakers say "make a mistake", never "do a mistake". Two or more words that regularly belong together like this are called…
questions.explanation: Words that occur together frequently are said to collocate, and the combination is a collocation: make a mistake, dark hair, first aid. An idiom is something else — its meaning cannot be worked out from its words, as in to give somebody a hand. A phrasal verb needs a verb plus an adverb or a preposition, as in to give up. And a synonym is simply another word with a similar meaning.

questions.prompt: Leila says her brother "burns the candle at both ends" the week before an exam. What does she mean?

options.text: He wastes his time instead of revising.
He loses his temper with everybody around him.
He spends far too much money on books.
He works very hard and stays up very late.

questions.explanation: To burn the candle at both ends means to work very hard and to stay up very late at night studying or working; the book gives to burn the midnight oil as its equivalent. A candle lit at both ends burns away twice as fast, and that picture is about energy spent — not about wasted time, not about anger, not about money. Knowing every word of the phrase still would not give you the meaning, and that is exactly what makes an expression idiomatic.

questions.prompt: In which of these words do the letters "ch" stand for the sound /k/, as in chemistry?
questions.explanation: Stomach ends with the /k/ sound, exactly like chemistry, psychology, chorus and ache. Machine has the /ʃ/ sound also heard in moustache, chores begins with the /tʃ/ sound of achievement, and the book groups spinach with /dʒ/. One spelling, four sounds: with ch the letters never tell you the pronunciation on their own, which is precisely why pronunciation dictionaries exist.

questions.prompt: An American visitor in London asks a passer-by where he can find "the elevator". Which British word is he looking for?
questions.explanation: American elevator is British lift — the same machine, two varieties of one language. The other words name other things: the pavement is where you walk beside the road, and Americans call it the sidewalk; the ground floor is what Americans call the first floor; and the stairs are climbed on foot. British and American English differ in accent, in spelling and, as here, in vocabulary.
